chapter: The Original Dixieland band to California
title: Why Hot Five records had no drums or bass
summary: Joe and Barry discuss how early recording equipment could not pick up drums and bass.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: It's kind of strange that the Hot Five rhythm section was just a banjo and a piano; it never featured any drums or bass.
Well, for one thing, on records in those days, those instruments didn't record, you know.
Oh, that's right, yeah. So I guess they figured, well, what's the point.
Although you could record like Baby Dodds on the Joe Oliver records; he just played those wood blocks on the cymbals.
It would pick things like that up. But it couldn't hardly pick up a bass drum or something like that, if you follow me.

I'm trying to think... With Louis, when they recorded the Hot Seven, which I think was 1927, they had this guy Pete Briggs on bass horn and Baby Dodds again played drums, and you could just about hear the drums and the bass on those records. So between, shall we say, '23 and '26, they must have developed some kind of technique that they could record these drums. Wasn't Gene Krupa or someone the first one they recorded a bass drum on or
something...? I read it in one of the books.

But it's strange, isn't it, that they couldn't record drums. I mean, drums is the noisiest instrument in the band if it's played noisily or loudly. Yet they didn't seem to be able to pick it up. It's weird.
The recording equipment just wasn't capable of doing it. If you had a good upright and a big old horn and blow in it, you see, and they couldn't get the drums close enough, was the whole thing...
